title: Forty Percent
subtitle: IV Fluid Allocation & Substitution Safety

brief.userPrompt: Monday, October 5, 2026, Fort Dodge. At 07:00 Brent Halvorsen (Purchasing and Inventory Manager) reads the morning report: on hand are 9.0 days of 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% (340 bags a day), 6.2 days of lactated Ringer's (120 a day) and 8 days of 250 mL minibags (410 a day). At 07:40 the primary wholesaler's allocation desk (800-555-0111) tells him that the manufacturer's main plant is down after a regional storm and that Prairie Ridge's allocation is cut to 40 percent of the usage of the baseline period for the next 4 weeks; the FDA lists the products as in shortage at 09:30. The exercise starts at 07:00 with Dr. Naomi Kessler (Director of Pharmacy), Priya Venkataraman (Clinical Pharmacy Manager), Tyrone Gaskill (Medication Safety Officer), CMO Dr. Amelia Nordstrom, CNO Gerald Whitcomb, Anesthesia Medical Director Dr. Lucas Hendrickx and PIO Ellen Sorensen. Pressure points: classifying the shortage as Level 2 or Level 3 using days on hand and allocation percent; setting the allocation percent for each service (ED, OR, ICU, medical-surgical, obstetrics, infusion center, long-term care unit) under the clinical priority order; conservation rules (oral first, IV push instead of minibags, no keep-vein-open infusions); approving the substitution of lactated Ringer's for sodium chloride 0.9% and an imported product with a different bag volume and port that the FDA has allowed under temporary importation, using the substitution checklist, with the pump library not yet updated; a secondary supplier offering 400 cases at 3 times the price without a lot list (a gray market question); a loan of 60 cases from Webster Valley Medical Center that arrives with a different label; the OR schedule on Wednesday with 11 elective joint replacement and abdominal cases and a 48-hour deferral decision when 1000 mL sodium chloride falls below 3 days on hand; the infusion center moving hydration appointments and a patient who cannot wait; an adverse event on 6 West when an imported 500 mL bag is run at the wrong rate; two units give conflicting instructions about flush volumes; a local TV reporter and a Facebook post claiming the hospital has run out of IV fluids and canceled surgeries; a physician demanding unrestricted fluids for sepsis boluses; reporting to the FDA shortage staff and the Iowa Board of Pharmacy; the 8-hour Drug Shortage Team meetings and the count of patients affected. The SimCell plays the wholesaler allocation desk, the manufacturer's customer service line, FDA drug shortage staff, the Iowa Board of Pharmacy, Webster Valley Medical Center and North Iowa Memorial Hospital pharmacies, the secondary supplier, the poison control center, physicians, patients and reporters.
audience: Clinical Pharmacy Manager / Medication Safety Officer
constraints: Every email address of the hospital uses the exercise domain prairieridgehealth.example; the wholesaler, manufacturer, other hospitals and the newspaper use fictional *.example domains; never a real company, hospital or newspaper domain; phone numbers are 515-555-01xx or 800-555-01xx.

FDA shortage listings and any importation letter are marked as exercise products; dose and conversion notes come only from the scenario and the plan, never invented; use the plan's shortage levels, priority order and substitution checklist as written; no real manufacturer is named as the cause.
Player roles are only those in the audience list; the Anesthesia Medical Director, ED Medical Director, OR Manager and other staff are played by the SimCell.

overview.theme: Making the Level 3 call from days on hand and allocation percent, rationing scarce IV fluids fairly by clinical priority, keeping substitutions safe when labels, bag volumes and the pump library don't match, and giving staff and the public one consistent message.
overview.threat: After a regional storm, the manufacturer's main IV fluid plant has gone down (no attacker is involved). On Monday, October 5, 2026 at 07:40, the primary wholesaler's allocation desk tells Prairie Ridge Health that for the next 4 weeks it will receive 40 percent of its baseline-period usage of 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9%, lactated Ringer's and 250 mL minibags. At 09:30 the FDA lists the products as in shortage. The 07:00 morning report already showed only 9.0 days of 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% (340 bags a day), 6.2 days of lactated Ringer's (120 a day) and 8 days of 250 mL minibags (410 a day). The cut runs through the pharmacy's perpetual inventory and 22 automated dispensing cabinets to the emergency department, operating rooms, ICU, medical-surgical units, obstetrics, the infusion center and the long-term care unit.
overview.operationalImpact: Within hours, days on hand fall at the central pharmacy and in the dispensing cabinets on nursing units. Nurses find cabinet pockets for 1000 mL bags and 250 mL minibags restricted, and they have to switch to oral routes, IV push in place of minibags and no keep-vein-open infusions. Two units send out conflicting instructions on flush volumes. Buyers must decide on a secondary supplier offering 400 cases at 3 times the price with no lot list. A 60-case loan from Webster Valley Medical Center arrives with a different label. An FDA-allowed imported product comes with a different bag volume and port, and the 240 smart infusion pumps don't have it in their library yet. On 6 West, an imported 500 mL bag is run at the wrong rate, causing an adverse event. Wednesday's OR schedule has 11 elective joint replacement and abdominal cases, and those patients may face a 48-hour deferral if 1000 mL sodium chloride falls below 3 days on hand. The infusion center is moving hydration appointments and has a patient who can't wait. A physician demands unrestricted fluids for sepsis boluses. A local TV reporter calls, and a Facebook post claims the hospital has run out of IV fluids and canceled surgeries. Patients and families are calling Patient Relations and the infusion center.

objectives.name: Decision Making
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to calculate days on hand for 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9%, lactated Ringer's and 250 mL minibags under the wholesaler's 40 percent allocation, recommend Level 3 activation to the Incident Commander, and set an internal allocation by percent of normal use and clinical priority, as Drug Shortage plan section 5 describes.

objectives.name: Use of Doctrine
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to apply the IV Fluid Conservation SOP (PH-22-A) and the Medication Safety Officer's substitution checklist (concentration, volume, labeling, pump library, look-alike risk, nursing education, second pharmacist check) before the Webster Valley loan and the FDA-allowed imported 500 mL bags reach the 22 dispensing cabinets and the 240 smart pumps, and to respond to the 6 West rate error.

objectives.name: Resource Management
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to decide whether to accept or refuse the secondary supplier's 400-case offer at 3 times the price with no lot list, to secure and document the loan agreement with neighboring hospitals, and to make the 48-hour elective surgery deferral decision for Wednesday's 11 cases against the 3-days-on-hand trigger.

objectives.name: Communication
objectives.text: Demonstrate the ability to issue one message with the same numbers to nursing units, the roughly 90 physicians on the medical staff and the public, ending the conflicting flush-volume instructions and correcting the false 'run out of IV fluids' Facebook post the same day with a statement signed off by the Incident Commander.

roles.name: Director of Pharmacy (Drug Shortage Team Chair)
roles.description: Owns the shortage level recommendation, the internal allocation by percent of normal use, loan agreements, spending authority and the briefing to the Incident Commander in Conference Room C.
standingOrders: Numbers First: every allocation and level call is based on current days on hand, worked out as on-hand divided by usage per day, never on the 07:00 report alone.
Protect the Protected: sepsis bundles, trauma resuscitation, burn care, diabetic ketoacidosis and hemorrhage are not restricted; any other use has to earn its share.
Sign Before Ship: no loaned or bought product enters stock until a signed loan agreement or a verified licensed source covers it.
One Voice Upward: the Incident Commander gets one consolidated pharmacy picture every 8 hours, not separate updates from each department.

roles.name: Pharmacy Purchasing and Inventory Manager
roles.team: Team B: Purchasing and Inventory Manager
roles.description: Owns wholesaler and manufacturer contact, allocation counts, the perpetual inventory, cabinet par levels and the search for loans and alternate suppliers.
standingOrders: Know the Source: refuse any offer that cannot show a lot list and a licensed chain of custody, however short the shelf is.
Count Twice: reconcile stockroom, dock, satellite and cabinet quantities by lot before reporting days on hand.
Ask Neighbors Early: call Webster Valley and the manufacturer's emergency allocation program on day one, not when stock hits 3 days.
Flag Every Difference: any product with a different label, bag volume or port goes to the Medication Safety Officer before put-away.

roles.name: Clinical Pharmacy Manager / Medication Safety Officer
roles.team: Team C: Clinical Pharmacy Manager / Medication Safety Officer
roles.description: Owns the conservation notice, activation of the substitution protocol in PH-22-A, the substitution checklist and the review of the 6 West adverse event.
standingOrders: Checklist Before Cabinet: no substitute product is loaded until concentration, volume, labeling, pump library, look-alike risk, nursing education and a second pharmacist check are all complete.
Speed vs. Safety: if the pump library is not updated, the substitute is not stocked on that unit, even when nurses are asking for it.
Plan Text Only: dose and conversion guidance comes from PH-22-A and the plan, never from improvised advice on the unit.
Stop and Review: after any substitution error, hold the product on all units until the cause is understood.

roles.name: Chief Medical Officer and P&T Chair
roles.description: Owns emergency P&T approvals, medical staff notification and the clinical arbitration of restrictions, including physician demands for exceptions.
standingOrders: Same Numbers: medical staff email, text and huddle scripts carry exactly the figures the Chief Nursing Officer sends to units.
Priority by Plan: settle physician demands against the clinical priority order and protected uses, not by who calls loudest.
Daily Must-Not-Wait List: require the ED and Anesthesia Medical Directors' list before each allocation reset.
Deferral Is Clinical: support elective deferral only when the 3-day trigger is met and urgent cases are protected.

roles.name: Chief Nursing Officer
roles.description: Owns unit notification, nursing education on conservation and substitutes, and ending conflicting unit-level instructions such as flush volumes.
standingOrders: One Unit Message: units follow only the CNO notice; local flush or fluid instructions are withdrawn when it is published.
Bedside Truth: if a bag, label or pump screen doesn't match the instruction, stop and call pharmacy before infusing.
Educate Before Exposure: no unit receives an imported or loaned product before its nurses have been briefed.
Report Without Blame: near misses and errors with substitutes are reported at once so other units can be warned.

roles.name: Public Information Officer (Director of Communications)
roles.description: Owns the holding, surgery-deferral and media statements, social media monitoring, and consistent messaging to patients, families, Patient Relations and local media.
standingOrders: Truth over Reassurance: say what continues (emergency, urgent surgery, obstetric care) and what may be rescheduled; never say the hospital is fine if it isn't.
No Blame by Name: never name a vendor or manufacturer as the cause unless the FDA or the manufacturer has done so publicly.
Correct Same Day: a false claim is answered the same day with a statement signed off by the Incident Commander.
All Calls to One Desk: physicians, nurses and staff send all media calls to ext. 3050.

phases.title: The Forty Percent Call
phases.goal: Tests whether the Drug Shortage Team spots the supply drop early, works out days on hand under the wholesaler's 40 percent allocation and escalates to the right shortage level before the information is complete.
beats: (07:00) The Purchasing Manager's 07:00 perpetual inventory check (Pharmacy Systems 2) shows 9.0 days on hand of 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% (340 bags/day), 6.2 days of lactated Ringer's (120/day) and 8 days of 250 mL minibags (410/day). A SimCell storeroom tech notes that the central stockroom pallets look light.

(07:40) The primary wholesaler's allocation desk (515-555-0142) calls, then confirms by email from allocations@wholesaler.example: 40 percent of baseline-period usage of 1000 mL NS, LR and 250 mL minibags for 4 weeks after a storm took the manufacturer's main plant offline. The notice names no manufacturer and gives no restart date.

Noise item: Nephrology asks whether CRRT and peritoneal dialysis solutions are affected. They fall outside PH-22-A and stay with Nephrology. Clinical Informatics also sends a routine reminder about the next pump library update for the 240 smart pumps.

First sign that the backup will not cover the gap: the buyer calls the secondary wholesaler, which says it is putting the same products on allocation for current customers only and cannot take new volume. Players have to calculate days on hand at 40 percent inbound supply and decide whether to recommend Level 2 conservation or Level 3 activation to the Incident Commander (Drug Shortage plan 5).

phases.title: Cabinets Running Dry
phases.goal: Tests whether the team can follow the shortage as it spreads through the 22 dispensing cabinets and the units, push back on false explanations and pressure from clinicians, and open Level 3 command with one set of numbers.
beats: (09:30, time jump) The FDA Drug Shortage Database lists 1000 mL NS, LR and 250 mL minibags as in shortage (marked EXERCISE). Cabinet pockets for 1000 mL bags and 250 mL minibags are restricted on nursing units. The ED, med-surg and the ICU report pockets at zero, and nurses are moving to oral routes, IV push instead of minibags and no keep-vein-open infusions under PH-22-A 2.

Red herring: the ED charge nurse (SimCell) insists the empty pockets are a cabinet or interface fault ('IT broke the pharmacy system') rather than the allocation, so part of the room starts troubleshooting. At the same time an ED physician demands unrestricted 1000 mL NS for sepsis boluses, which tests the priority order in Drug Shortage plan 6.

Visual for the room: the daily shortage report on the Conference Room C screen (ext. 3690) shows days on hand falling by location. Two unit memos are shown side by side with conflicting flush-volume instructions.

The public notices: a Facebook community group post claims 'Prairie Ridge has run out of IV fluids and cancelled surgeries.' A local TV reporter calls the PIO at ext. 3050. Patients start calling Patient Relations and the infusion center.
Manufacturer customer service (800-555-0167) gives an 'estimated' plant restart in 7–10 days, which conflicts with the wholesaler's 4-week allocation. Nobody in the room trusts it for planning.

phases.title: Defer or Operate
phases.goal: Tests the single high-consequence call: whether to defer Wednesday's 11 elective cases for 48 hours on the days-on-hand trigger, plus the supply and messaging decisions that follow from it.
beats: DECISION POINT (Tuesday 07:00, time jump): the projection shows 1000 mL NS falling below 3 days on hand before Wednesday. The Anesthesia Medical Director and OR Manager (SimCell) present 11 elective joint replacement and abdominal cases. The CMO and Director of Pharmacy must recommend to the Incident Commander whether to defer them for 48 hours (Drug Shortage plan 5, step 5), which strands patients who have already arranged their care and loses revenue, and running them on the current supply, which uses up the reserve for ED and ICU priorities.

The secondary supplier (sales@secondsource-med.example) offers 400 cases at 3 times the price with no lot list. Under Drug Shortage plan 4 the buyer and the Director of Pharmacy must check the supplier's licensure and either refuse it as gray market or document why they accept it.

Webster Valley Medical Center confirms a 60-case loan. The bags arrive with a different label, so the Medication Safety Officer must run the substitution checklist before they reach any cabinet, and the loan agreement has to be documented. The infusion center reschedules hydration patients but flags one patient whose dose cannot be delayed, which tests priority 5 in Drug Shortage plan 6.

Media pressure with a deadline: the TV reporter will air at 17:00 with or without comment. The PIO must have the holding statement and the deferred-surgery statement (Clinical plan 5) signed off by the Incident Commander. The CNO and CMO need to send one message with the same numbers to units and roughly 90 physicians, which ends the conflicting flush-volume instructions.

phases.title: Imported Bags, New Risk
phases.goal: Tests safe use of replacement product: verifying the FDA-allowed imported bags before they reach the smart pumps, responding to the 6 West rate error and completing the required notifications before ENDEX.
beats: (Wednesday, time jump) FDA-allowed imported 500 mL bags (EXERCISE importation letter) arrive with a different bag volume and port. Clinical Informatics says the 240-pump library will not include the product until a later build. The Clinical Pharmacy Manager must handle the conversion and the full checklist, including the second pharmacist check and nurse education, before the bags are loaded into cabinets.

Things go wrong again: on 6 West an imported 500 mL bag is run at the wrong rate and the patient has an adverse event. The room must quarantine or hold the stock, check the other units, report through the medication event system and decide whether the event is serious enough for FDA MedWatch and ISMP (Drug Shortage plan 8).

A partial recovery is claimed: the wholesaler says the plant is restarting in stages and the allocation may rise. Players have to verify it against actual receipts and days on hand before they relax allocation or reinstate elective cases.

Notifications and close-out: FDA Drug Shortage Staff via the CDER shortage email, the Iowa Board of Pharmacy for the import use, a P&T Committee written report due within 7 days, and the metrics for the 8-hour meeting (days on hand, allocation percent, patients affected, substitutions and checklist pass rate, adverse events) recorded with the same numbers as the messages. The PIO issues the next scheduled update, followed by the after-action hot wash and ENDEX.

hotwash.methodDescription: Ask the room for three things that went well and three things that broke or failed during the exercise. Go around the room one team at a time (pharmacy, nursing, OR and anesthesia, PIO, command) and write every item on the whiteboard in two columns before anyone discusses them.

questions.text: At I-01 the 07:00 perpetual inventory showed 9.0 days on hand for NS 1000 mL. At the stockroom door, Tyler Bergstrom told you the back pallets looked light and the dock pallets hadn't been scanned. At I-08 the lot recount dropped the figure to 2,560 bags and 7.5 days, and the dock pallets turned out to be D5W. When did you stop trusting the system figure? Which number did you use for your Level 3 recommendation and your percent-of-normal-use allocation? What would have made you order a physical count before you signed off on the morning report?

At I-12, Dr. Lucas Hendrickx and Denise Aldrich needed a yes or no by 11:00 on Wednesday's 11 elective cases. Their projection showed NS dropping to 2.96 days on hand by Wednesday morning. Did you decide against the 3-days-on-hand trigger, or against the pressure from patients who had arranged rides, rehab beds and family travel? Who signed the written deferral? What information would have let you decide before anesthesia had to ask?

The 6 West rate error and the imported 500 mL bags tested whether a substitution can reach the 22 dispensing cabinets and 240 smart pumps before the pump library, labels and nursing education are ready. Did you run the Medication Safety Officer's checklist, including the second pharmacist check, before the Webster Valley loan and the imported product were released? When the rate error came in, did you treat it as evidence that the substitution process had failed, or as an incident ticket to close? Did pharmacy and the bedside nurses understand each other on bag volume and pump settings?

You were offered 400 cases from a secondary supplier at three times the price, with no lot list. You were also negotiating a loan from neighboring hospitals. How did you decide whether to accept or refuse the 400 cases? Who owned that decision? Was the Webster Valley loan agreement documented before any product moved? When did you bring in the wholesaler, the neighboring hospitals and the Iowa Department of Public Health, which wanted your status by noon? Would earlier contact have changed your options?

By mid-morning, staff were working from conflicting instructions. Memo A (6 West) said no KVO and one prefilled flush syringe. Memo B (ICU) said to draw flushes from a bedside 250 mL bag and keep KVO running. At the same time, the public saw the 'RUN OUT of IV fluids' post at I-09 and the 'foreign IV bag' post at I-17b. North Iowa NewsChannel wanted someone on camera at noon, and patient relations was taking calls. What did you tell staff, physicians and the public before you had confirmed numbers? Did all three groups get the same days-on-hand figures? How long did it take to get a corrected statement signed off by the Incident Commander?

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Primary wholesaler allocation desk rep, also playing the manufacturer customer service rep it passes calls to (vendor / service provider)
simcellScripts.trigger: The Purchasing and Inventory Manager or Director of Pharmacy calls the allocation desk ((800-555-0111) to ask for more than 40 percent, an emergency shipment or a restart date, or calls about the 60 percent update email (I-18).
hardQuestions: "What's your account number and the PO number for the order you're asking about? I can't look anything up without it."

"You're asking for an exception to the 40 percent. Send me your current days on hand and patient-care impact in writing, on letterhead, signed by the Director of Pharmacy. Every hospital in the state says it's an emergency."
"Our 4-hour emergency delivery only covers allocated quantities. Have you already ordered against this week's 952? If you have, there's nothing left for me to send."
"About the 60 percent: the email said MAY. Do you see a confirmed quantity on your open orders? No? Then the answer is still 40 percent."
concessions: Once a written request arrives with days on hand and patient-care impact, the rep opens a case number and files it for the manufacturer's emergency allocation program (a few cases, no promised ship date).

If players ask, the rep confirms in writing that Thursday 05:30 carries 952 NS 1000 mL and that no increase is confirmed. That gives players a document to stop the push to put electives back on the schedule.
If players commit to standing orders at exactly the allocated amount, the rep agrees to call the Purchasing Manager directly when allocation review results come out.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Webster Valley Medical Center pharmacy buyer, Fort Dodge (neighboring hospital lending product)
simcellScripts.trigger: The Purchasing Manager calls 515-555-0164 to request a loan, or calls back about the 60 cases delivered to the dock (I-14).
hardQuestions: "I emailed the loan form an hour ago. Until it's signed by someone with authority, those 720 bags are still on our books. Who's signing on your end, and when?"
"We need one-for-one replacement in 30 days: same product, 1000 mL. If your Thursday truck is only 952 for the week, how are you paying us back?"
"You want more? We're on allocation too. Tell me how many days on hand you really have before I go back to my director."
concessions: Once the Director of Pharmacy signs the loan agreement, the buyer emails the lot and NDC detail for lot WV-88213 so pharmacy can build the product in its system and check it against the substitution checklist.
If players agree to repay with the same product or to a written repayment schedule, the buyer agrees to stretch repayment to 45 days.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Iowa Board of Pharmacy inspector (state regulator); if players contact them, the same Controller also plays FDA drug shortage staff and the Iowa Department of Public Health
simcellScripts.trigger: The inspector calls (515-555-0172) at I-19, or players contact the Board, the FDA's CDER shortage mailbox or the Iowa Department of Public Health about the imported product, the loan or the 6 West event.
hardQuestions: "Has the temporarily imported product been labeled for your staff? Who did the dose and label conversion, and is it documented?"
"You told me there was a patient event. When did it happen, has it been reported internally, and has anyone told the FDA? Why am I hearing this from you at 10:50 when it happened at 10:15?"
"Is any of the imported lot still on a unit shelf right now? How many bags, and where are the two missing cases?"
"The Department of Public Health asked for your regional status by noon. Will the numbers you send them match what you've told me?"
concessions: If players give a written notification that states the lot, the label differences, the hold on every unit, the event and the corrective actions, the inspector accepts it as timely and schedules a follow-up rather than an on-site visit today.

If the hospital confirms imported bags will be released only after the checklist, a second pharmacist check, nurse education and the pump library build, the inspector agrees the import use can continue.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Ryan Teasdale, assignment desk, North Iowa NewsChannel (local TV); the same Controller may play the health reporter from the Fort Dodge daily newspaper
simcellScripts.trigger: The PIO calls back about the 08:38 or 09:16 media slip (I-09, I-12b), or answers the newspaper reporter's email (I-03b), or the 10:24 Facebook post gets the station tagged (I-17b).
hardQuestions: "Simple question: did Prairie Ridge run out of IV fluids, yes or no? I have a woman on camera saying it did."
"Is her dad's knee replacement Wednesday cancelled? How many surgeries are you cancelling?"
"Which company's plant went down? Everyone online is saying the name. Confirm it or we'll report what's out there."
"I need something by 15:00 to edit for the 17:00 package. Can someone go on camera, and who?"
concessions: If the PIO gives a statement before the deadline, the reporter runs the hospital's numbers and the line 'emergency, urgent surgery and obstetric care continue' next to the family's claim. The statement must say a national shortage, emergency, urgent surgery and obstetric care continue, some elective procedures may be rescheduled, who patients should call, and when the next update is.
If the PIO offers a named spokesperson and a time for the next update, the reporter drops the request to name the manufacturer for tonight's package.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Dr. Marcus Feld, ED attending physician
simcellScripts.trigger: The CMO or Director of Pharmacy returns the I-07b call, or players announce restrictions or an allocation that affects the ED.
hardQuestions: "I've got a septic patient in Bay 6 who needs a bolus. Who exactly do I call at 3 a.m. when the pocket is locked? Give me a name and an extension, not a policy."
"You say the ED is a priority. What percent of normal use am I getting? Why is that number different from what the charge nurse just told me?"
"If you won't give me unrestricted fluids, put the restriction in writing with the CMO's name on it."
concessions: If the CMO explains the clinical priority tier in writing, with a guaranteed override path for sepsis and resuscitation, the attending accepts the restriction on non-emergent uses. That includes no KVO and oral hydration where possible.
Once players send the single page with days on hand, the allocation percent and the next update time, the attending agrees to brief the ED physicians at the next huddle using those numbers.

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment. Capabilities, plans and procedures are being evaluated, not individual Drug Shortage Team members.
The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented. Supplier figures, inventory counts and days-on-hand values in the injects are accepted as given unless an inject corrects them.

Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies and procedures: the Drug Shortage plan, the IV Fluid Conservation SOP (PH-22-A), the Clinical Operations plan and the Pharmacy plan. Where a plan is silent, players state how they would decide and who has authority.
Players have only the information in the narrative and injects. They do not assume information about the supply disruption's cause, duration or restart date that they have not been given.
Decisions made in one module carry into later modules. Where the scenario has to assume an outcome to move forward, the facilitator will state it.
artificialities: Time is compressed. Each module covers about one hour of discussion, and there are time jumps between modules, including a two-day jump from Monday, October 5 to Wednesday, October 7, 2026, before Module 4.

The Simulation Cell (SimCell) plays everyone outside the room: the primary and secondary wholesalers, the manufacturer, the alternate supplier, Webster Valley Medical Center, the importer, the FDA Drug Shortage Staff, the Iowa Board of Pharmacy, the Iowa Department of Public Health, the Incident Commander's office, Anesthesia and the OR, unit charge nurses, Clinical Informatics, Patient Relations, the media and community social media users.

The pharmacy system, the EHR link, the 22 automated dispensing cabinets, the 240 smart pumps and their drug library, the medication event system and the medical staff email list are referred to as the plans describe them. No live system is accessed or changed.

Injects are delivered on paper or on screen as simulated phone calls, emails, status boards, memos and social media posts. All FDA, importer and supplier documents are exercise products, and all NDCs and lot numbers are fictional.
Physical work such as lot recounts, quarantine tagging, receiving at the dock and clinical care at the bedside happens through injects and is described rather than performed.

**Module 1: The Forty Percent Call (07:00–08:00, Monday, October 5, 2026)**

It is 07:00 on Monday, October 5, 2026, in Fort Dodge, Webster County, Iowa. A regional line of storms crossed the Midwest overnight. This morning in Fort Dodge it is clearing and cool, 48°F, with no local power or road problems.

Prairie Ridge Health is running a normal Monday. 104 of 118 beds are occupied and 8 of 10 ICU beds are filled. The ED had 31 visits overnight, the OR has 14 cases booked across its 5 rooms, and the infusion center opens at 08:00 with 22 appointments. The primary wholesaler's 05:30 delivery arrived on schedule. The pharmacy system, the EHR link and all 22 automated dispensing cabinets are up. There are no active IV fluid shortages, and the status is **NORMAL**. The morning perpetual inventory report is being run in the stockroom.

How early to escalate, and to which shortage level, when supplier information is incomplete
Giving the Incident Commander one pharmacy recommendation instead of several

**Module 2: Cabinets Running Dry (08:00–09:00, Monday, October 5, 2026)**

It is 08:00. The 07:00 perpetual inventory report showed 1000 mL sodium chloride 0.9% at 3,060 bags (9.0 days on hand), lactated Ringer's at 744 bags (6.2 days) and 250/100 mL minibags at 3,280 (8.0 days). The storeroom technician then reported that the back two NS pallets look only half full. He also noted that two pallets from the 05:30 truck are sitting on the dock unscanned, and he offered to count by lot. Nephrology called about CRRT supplies after families saw news of a storm-damaged IV plant. Clinical Informatics reminded staff that change requests for Thursday's smart pump library update are due Tuesday at noon.

At 07:40 the primary wholesaler put Prairie Ridge on **40 percent** of baseline-period usage for four weeks, with no restart date given. The weekly allocation is 952 NS 1000 mL, 336 LR and 1,148 NS 250 mL minibags, and orders above that are cut at order entry. The secondary wholesaler in Des Moines will not add new volume and offered only a waitlist. A newspaper health reporter wants a comment by 14:00. The Incident Commander, Dale Pruitt, wants one Level 2 or Level 3 recommendation from pharmacy by **08:15**.

The 07:30 cabinet restock went out short. NS 1000 mL and minibag pockets now show RESTRICTED, and the ED, the medical-surgical units and the ICU each have at least one cabinet with zero 1000 mL NS. Nurses are improvising in different ways: oral hydration, IV push instead of piggybacks, and stopping keep-vein-open lines. Unit huddles start at 08:30.

**Module 3: Defer or Operate (09:00–10:00, Monday, October 5, 2026)**

It is 09:00. The Incident Commander, Dale Pruitt, has opened the command center in Conference Room C (ext. 3690), and the Drug Shortage Team is at the table for its opening huddle. The first full Level 3 meeting is set for 11:00, then every 8 hours. A lot recount at 08:20 found the two back NS pallets each about 250 bags short. The unscanned dock pallets turned out to be D5W, not NS. The recount showed LR at 5.8 days on hand and minibags at 7.4 days.

At 08:40 the manufacturer put lot NS-26-0917A (890 bags) on hold for incomplete sterilization records, and it is tagged DO NOT USE – QUARANTINE. Usable 1000 mL NS is now **1,660 bags, 4.9 days on hand** at an average daily use of 340. The manufacturer estimates a plant restart in 7 to 10 days but will not commit to it. The FDA will list the three products as in shortage at 09:30. The first allocated wholesaler truck (952 NS) is not due until Thursday at 05:30.

Pressure is building inside and outside the hospital. The ED charge nurse blamed an IT failure and asked for cabinet overrides. An ED attending demanded unrestricted NS. 6 West and the ICU issued conflicting flush memos: prefilled syringes on 6 West, and flushes drawn from an opened 250 mL bag in the ICU. Both memos are still in use, and no single notice has gone out to units or physicians. A community Facebook post claims Prairie Ridge has "RUN OUT of IV fluids" and is cancelling surgeries. A TV station wants someone on camera, and Patient Relations has logged 19 calls, many from Wednesday surgery and infusion patients.

Whether to accept an urgent, high-priced offer of NS from an unfamiliar supplier

Who decides individual patient priority when a protocol needs restricted fluids
Replacing conflicting unit memos with one message and answering a false public post the same day

**Module 4: Imported Bags, New Risk (10:00–11:00, Wednesday, October 7, 2026)**

It is 10:00 on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, two days later. Wednesday's OR is running on the schedule set on Monday. Conservation is in force on every unit under the single CNO notice. The 07:00 recount shows usable NS 1000 mL at 1,120 bags. Use over the last 24 hours was 260 bags a day, so days on hand is **4.3**. LR is at 4.9 days and minibags at 5.6 days. Lot NS-26-0917A (890 bags) is still in quarantine. The 720 bags Webster Valley loaned on Monday are still on hold in receiving: the signed loan agreement and proof that the transfer is covered by Webster Valley's pharmacy license never came back, so they are not in this count.

At 08:45 the first relief arrived on the dock: 80 cases (1,600 bags) of imported 0.9% sodium chloride **500 mL** bags that the FDA is allowing under temporary importation. The bags have a foreign-language primary label, a different bag volume and a different administration port. The ICU, the ED and 6 West have each called pharmacy to ask when they can have them. The Thursday 05:30 allocated truck (952 NS) is still the only confirmed wholesaler delivery. The next 8-hour Drug Shortage Team meeting is at 11:00 in Conference Room C (ext. 3690).
